title: Where am I, and what is here?
objectives: Use `pwd`, `ls` and `cd` to move around your machine.
Read a relative path with `..` and an absolute path with `~` from any folder.
Save typing with Tab completion and the up arrow.

screens.prose:
A terminal is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. On a Mac it is the Terminal app; on Windows, install WSL or Git Bash first. Ana now works on her Mac, so her home is `/Users/ana`. Someone typed `pwd` and pressed Enter, and the machine replied:

```sh
$ pwd
/Users/ana/data
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured.

screens.question: Tap the folder this terminal is working in.

hints.text: Read the reply from left to right. Each slash steps one folder down.
The path starts at /, the top of the tree.
/ then Users, then ana, then data. The last name is where the terminal is.

feedback.correct: The path ends at data, so that is where the terminal is.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the path down from / to its last name.

byKey.home: You tapped ana. The path carries on past ana to data, one folder deeper.
byKey.top: You tapped /, where the path starts. The terminal is at the end of the path, not the start.
byKey.prices: prices.csv is a file. The path stops at data, the folder that holds it.

explain.text: You followed the path from / down to its last name, data. `pwd` means print working directory: the folder the terminal is working in. Directory is the older word for folder.

screens.prose:
The terminal now works in ana, ringed in blue. Next you type `ls`, short for list. Before it replies, predict what it shows.

```sh
$ ls
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: Tap every item you expect `ls` to print.

hints.text: ls lists the working folder. What hangs directly below ana?
These four hang straight off ana.

feedback.correct: ls shows the four items directly inside ana.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only what sits one level below ana.

byKey.deep: You also tapped prices.csv and backtest. They sit inside data and projects, one level further down.
byKey.folders: You left out notes.txt. ls lists files as well as folders.
byKey.prices: prices.csv is inside data, not directly inside ana. ls does not look that deep.
byKey.backtest: backtest is inside projects, not directly inside ana. ls does not look that deep.
byKey.users: Users is above ana. ls looks inside the working folder, not up.

explain.text: ls printed four names: Downloads, data, notes.txt and projects. It stops one level down, so prices.csv stays hidden inside data. To see it, you have to look inside data.

screens.prose:
Here is the whole exchange so far, plus one new line. The dollar sign is the **prompt**: the shell is waiting for you. On a Mac it is usually `%` instead, and you never type either. What you type after it is a **command**. What the machine prints back is the **output**.

```sh
$ pwd
/Users/ana
$ ls
Downloads  data  notes.txt  projects
$ ls data
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: What does `ls data` print?

options.why: You expected ls to repeat the name you gave it. A folder name after ls means: list what is inside this folder.
You ignored the word after ls. Without it ls lists the working folder; with data it lists inside data.
That is a path, the kind of thing pwd prints. ls prints names, not paths.

hints.text: The word after ls tells it which folder to look in.
Look at what is inside data.
data holds one file, prices.csv. That is all ls can show.

feedback.correct: ls looked inside data and found one file.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List what is inside data, not what is around it.

explain.text: The word after `ls` told it which folder to list, so it printed what is inside data. You did not move: you looked into data from ana. Every exchange has the same three parts: prompt, command, output.

screens.prose:
`ls` looks; `cd` moves. It stands for change directory. You are in ana again and type:

```sh
$ cd projects
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: Tap the folder you are in now.

hints.text: cd moves the working folder to the one you name.
projects hangs directly below ana.
The blue ring moves from ana down to projects.

feedback.correct: cd moved you one level down, into projects.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the working folder to the folder you named.

byKey.stay: You stayed in ana. That is what ls would do; cd actually moves you.
byKey.deep: You went two levels down. cd projects stops at projects; backtest would need cd projects/backtest.

explain.text: cd projects moved the working folder down into projects. cd prints nothing when it works, so silence means success. Type pwd whenever you want to check where you are.

screens.prose:
Two dots, `..`, mean the folder one level up: the parent. You are in projects and type:

```sh
$ cd ../data
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: Tap where you end up.

hints.text: Read the path one piece at a time, from left to right.
The two dots take you from projects up to ana.
Up to ana, then down into data.

feedback.correct: Up one level to ana, then down into data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the pieces in order: first up, then down.

byKey.up-only: You stopped after the two dots. The path carries on: up to ana, then down into data.
byKey.stay: You stayed in projects. The two dots take you up and out of it first.
byKey.backtest: backtest is inside projects. The two dots go up, away from it.
byKey.prices: prices.csv is a file, and the path ends at data. cd can only stop at a folder.

explain.text: You went up one level to ana, then down into data. A path like ../data is read one piece at a time, starting from where you are. That is what makes it a relative path.

screens.prose:
The tilde, `~`, is a shortcut for your home folder, here /Users/ana. You are in data and type two commands:

```sh
$ cd ~/projects/backtest
$ pwd
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: What does `pwd` print?

options.why: You started from data. A path that begins with ~ starts from home, wherever you are.
You copied the path you typed. pwd always prints the full path, starting from /.
You dropped the home folder. ~ stands for /Users/ana, so that goes in front.

hints.text: Where does a path that starts with ~ begin?
~ is ana, your home folder.
From ana, down to projects, then down to backtest. pwd writes that out in full from /.

feedback.correct: The ~ sent you home first, then down to backtest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start the path at home, then write the result in full from /.

explain.text: The ~ sent you to /Users/ana first, so starting in data did not matter. pwd prints the full path from the top, /. A path that starts with / or ~ is absolute: it means the same place from anywhere.

screens.prose:
You are home, in ana. You want to look at the prices, so you type:

```sh
$ cd data/prices.csv
```

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: What happens?

options.text: You move into prices.csv and can see the prices
options.why: You treated the file as a place. cd only enters folders; a file is something you read, not somewhere you stand.

options.text: An error saying it is not a directory, and you stay in ana
You end up in data, next to the file
options.why: You expected cd to get as far as it can. When cd fails, it does not move you at all.

options.text: The file opens in a spreadsheet
options.why: cd never opens files. It only changes the working folder.

hints.text: Is prices.csv a folder or a file?
prices.csv is a file, coloured on the tree.
cd needs a folder at the end of its path. Given a file, it refuses.

feedback.correct: cd refuses, and you stay in ana.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what cd does when the path ends at a file.

byKey.inside: You tried to stand inside a file. cd enters folders only, so it prints an error instead.
byKey.halfway: You expected cd to stop at data. A failed cd leaves you exactly where you started.

explain.text: On a Mac the shell replies `cd: not a directory: data/prices.csv`, and the blue ring stays on ana. Folders are entered; files are read. Reading a file takes a different command, coming two lessons from now.

screens.prose: Typing names in full is slow, and one typo breaks the command. Press the **Tab** key part-way through a name and the shell finishes it. You are in ana, type `cd pro`, then press Tab.

state.caption: Folders are plain circles; files are coloured. The blue ring is where the terminal is.

screens.question: What does the line read after Tab?

options.why: prices.csv lives inside data. Tab only completes from names in the folder you are typing into, here ana.

options.text: `cd pro`, unchanged: Tab only completes command names
options.why: Tab completes file and folder names too. That is where it saves the most typing.
Tab finishes one name per press. Press it again to complete the next level down.

hints.text: Which names in ana start with pro?
Only one item in ana starts with those letters.
Tab fills in the rest of projects and adds a slash, because it is a folder.

feedback.correct: Only projects matches, so Tab finishes it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for names in ana that start with pro.

explain.text: Tab looked in ana, found one name starting with pro, and finished it with a slash. If several names match, Tab lists them: at once in zsh on a Mac, on a second press in bash. The up arrow does the same job for whole commands: it brings back the last one you ran.

screens.prose:
Every move you made used the same few commands:

```sh
$ pwd
$ ls
$ ls data
$ cd data
$ cd ..
$ cd ~
```

In order: print the working folder, list it, list inside data, move into data, move up one level, go home. A path is read piece by piece from where you are, unless it starts with `/` or `~`.
screens.question: Build the relative path that takes `cd` from backtest to data.

hints.text: How many levels up is the first folder that holds data?
data hangs off ana, two levels above backtest.
Up to projects, up to ana, then down into data.

feedback.correct: Two levels up to ana, then down into data: `cd ../../data`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the steps up to ana, then add the step down.

byKey.p: You went back down into projects. From backtest you need to climb, not descend.
byKey.b: You named backtest, which is where you already are. Paths start from here, so start climbing.

explain.text: From backtest, one `../` reaches projects and a second reaches ana. Then data steps down into the folder you want. So `cd ../../data` works, and so does the absolute `cd ~/data`.

screens.prose: Your broker sends a CSV of each day's trades, and you save each one to ~/Downloads. You are working in ~/projects/backtest. You want to see which exports have arrived, without leaving backtest.

state.caption: You are in backtest. The exports are in Downloads.

screens.question: Which command lists them?

options.why: That path is relative, so ls looks for a Downloads folder inside backtest. There is none, so you get an error.
cd would move you, which you did not want. The relative path also fails from backtest.
One `../` only climbs to projects. Downloads hangs off ana, two levels up.

hints.text: Is Downloads inside backtest?
Downloads hangs off ana, your home folder.
Start the path from home with ~, and it works from any folder.

feedback.correct: A ~ path finds Downloads from anywhere.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name Downloads by a path that works from backtest.

explain.text: Starting with ~ makes the path absolute, so it works from any folder. `ls ../../Downloads` also works, but only from backtest. For folders you use every day, ~ paths are the safer habit.

ideas: `pwd` prints where you are, `ls` lists what is there, and `cd` moves you.
A path is read piece by piece from where you are. `..` is one level up and `~` is home.
Tab finishes names and the up arrow brings back old commands, so you rarely type in full.

formula.name: Reading a path
formula.note: A path that starts with / or ~ is absolute and works from anywhere.

summary.trap: cd only enters folders. Given a file, it prints an error and you stay where you were.

quiz.prose:
You are at the very top of the tree, the folder `/`. You type two commands:

```sh
$ cd ..
$ pwd
```
quiz.question: What does `pwd` print?

options.why: You expected an error. At the top, `..` points back to / itself, so cd stays put quietly.
You went down. `..` always moves up, and from / there is nowhere higher.

feedback.correct: At the top, up leads nowhere new.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is above /.

explain.text: / has no parent, so its `..` is itself. cd moves you nowhere and prints nothing. pwd still prints /.

quiz.prose: A minute ago you ran `ls ~/Downloads`. A new export should have arrived since.
quiz.question: What is the quickest way to run the same command again?

options.text: Press the up arrow, then Enter

options.why: Tab finishes a name you are typing. It does not bring back old commands.
pwd prints where you are. It does not repeat anything.

feedback.correct: The up arrow brings back your last command.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which key recalls earlier commands?

explain.text: Each press of the up arrow steps back one command in your history. Enter runs it again. You can also edit it first.

quiz.prose:
Your home folder is /Users/ana. You are in /Users/ana/projects/backtest and type:

```sh
$ cd ../..
$ pwd
```
quiz.question: What does `pwd` print?

options.why: You climbed one level. Each `..` is one step up, and there are two.
You climbed three levels. Count the pairs of dots: there are two.
You read the dots as staying here. One dot means here; two dots mean up.

feedback.correct: Two steps up from backtest is ana.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count one step up per `..`.

explain.text: The first `..` climbs to projects and the second to ana. pwd prints it in full: /Users/ana.

quiz.prose: Your home folder holds a folder called data.
quiz.question: Which path names that folder correctly from any working folder?

options.why: A bare name is relative. It only works when you are already in your home folder.
This is relative too. It works only from a folder one level below home.

feedback.correct: A path that starts with ~ is absolute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the path that does not depend on where you are.

explain.text: ~/data starts from home, so it means the same folder from anywhere. data and ../data both start from wherever you happen to be.
